::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

- Choose between `multiext()`, `directory()` and a `.done` sentinel for a step that writes many files.
- Split a step into chunks with `scattergather:` and gather the results.
- Say when a checkpoint is needed, and when it is not.
- Predict what reruns after you change a parameter, and control it with `--forcerun`, `--until` and `--rerun-triggers`.
- Request a GPU for one rule from the profile.

Time: 45 min
:::

## When "one file per step" stops fitting

Until now every rule wrote a file or two with names you could write down.
Three kinds of step break that:

- a tool writes a set of files you do not want to list (`bowtie2-build`);
- one big job is faster as many small ones (aligning a deep FASTQ);
- you only know how many outputs there are after a job has run.

Each has its own tool. The first two are common in the lab pipelines. The third
is rare, and none of them needs it.

## One step, many files

`bowtie2-build` writes six index files that share a prefix. RegPipe has
declared them two ways.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### `multiext()` (stopA-C)

{{< snippet repo="stopC" file="workflows/rules/align.smk" rule="bowtie2_index" >}}

### `directory()` (stopD)

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/align.smk" rule="bowtie2_index" >}}

### `.done` (ChromSimPipe)

{{< snippet repo="chromsimpipe" file="workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile" rule="preparePolysim" >}}

:::

## Which to use

| | `multiext()` | `directory()` | `.done` sentinel |
|---|---|---|---|
| You list | every file | the folder | one marker file |
| Snakemake checks | every file exists | the folder exists | the marker exists |
| Delete one index file | rerun | **nothing happens** | **nothing happens** |
| Folder made for you | yes | no (`mkdir -p`) | only the marker's |
| Breaks if the tool renames its files | yes (`.bt2l` for genomes over 4 Gb) | no | no |

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
We tried the "delete one file" row. In a stopC copy, removing
`genome.rev.2.bt2` makes the dry run say
`reason: Missing output files: output/reference/bowtie2_index/genome.rev.2.bt2`.
In stopD, removing `genome.1.bt2` from the `directory()` output gives
`Nothing to be done`, and the next `align` would fail.

So `multiext()` is the safest when you know the names. `directory()` is
convenient when you do not, and Snakemake does not create the folder for you,
which is why stopD's shell command starts with `mkdir -p {output}`. A sentinel
says only "this step ran". ChromSimPipe uses one for nearly every step, because
its steps write into folders shared by many jobs, or write nothing Snakemake
should track (see [Sentinels](../field-guide/chromsimpipe.qmd#cs-sentinels)).
The cost is that Snakemake can no longer tell you when a real file is missing.
:::

## Pointing at another rule's output

`align` needs the index. Instead of repeating the path, it names the rule:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/align.smk" lines="68-71" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`rules.bowtie2_index.output` is whatever that rule declares: the six files in
stopC, the folder in stopD. When the declaration changed, `align` did not need
editing. The one condition is that `bowtie2_index` must be defined before
`align` (module 6). ChromSimPipe's `mergeShards` does the same with `expand()`:
it asks for one `simulateShard` marker per shard, built from that rule's output
pattern.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .exercise}

## Scatter-gather

The course FASTQs are small, but a real ChIP-seq library can take hours to
align as one job. RegPipe can split each FASTQ into chunks, align each chunk as
its own job, and merge. Set `scatter_chunks: 4` in the config:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/align.smk" lines="90-112" >}}

## Gather

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/align.smk" rule="merge_chunks" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`scattergather: chunks = SCATTER` creates two helpers. `scatter.chunks(pattern)`
expands `{scatteritem}` to `1-of-4`, `2-of-4`, ... `4-of-4` and returns the list
of files; `gather.chunks(pattern)` does the same for the input of the merge.
`{{sample}}` has double braces so it survives that expansion and stays a
wildcard. `merge_chunks` writes the same `_aligned.bam` that `align` would have
written, so `filter` and everything after it do not know whether scatter was
on.

The whole block sits under `if SCATTER == 0: ... else:`, a switch from module 6.
With `scatter_chunks: 0` (the default) the `align` rule exists and the three
scatter rules do not.
:::

## 61 jobs become 111

{{< generated name="regpipe-dryrun-scatter4" lines="3-20" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The ten `align` jobs are replaced by 10 `split_fastq`, 40 `align_chunk` and
10 `merge_chunks` jobs: 61 - 10 + 60 = 111. Nothing else changes.

Are the results the same? We ran the full pipeline both ways. The QC table is
byte-identical and the peaks are identical. The one thing that can differ is
which copy of a duplicate read `samtools markdup` keeps, because the merged BAM
can order reads at the same position differently. The number of reads kept is
the same.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .exercise}

## ChromSimPipe shards by hand

ChromSimPipe splits each simulation into `N_SHARDS` independent runs, without
`scattergather:`. The shard is an ordinary wildcard:

{{< snippet repo="chromsimpipe" file="workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile" rule="simulateShard" >}}

{{< snippet repo="chromsimpipe" file="workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile" rule="mergeShards" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
It is the same idea: one job per `{shard}`, and a gather rule whose input is an
`expand()` over `range(N_SHARDS)`. The difference is that the script does the
splitting (`--shard-index`, `--n-shards`) and every output is a `.done` marker.
`scattergather:` is tidier when Snakemake can make the chunks itself, as with a
FASTQ. A hand-rolled wildcard is just as good when the program splits its own
work.
:::

## Checkpoints

Sometimes the number of outputs depends on the data. Snakemake builds the
whole job graph before it runs anything, so it needs a way to stop, look, and
add jobs. That is a checkpoint.

None of the lab pipelines has one. RegPipe does not need one either: the number
of samples, chunks and targets all come from the samplesheet and the config.
Here is a small example on the course data, to show the mechanics. `split -l 50`
cuts the RAD21 peak file into files of 50 peaks, and you do not know how many
files until it has run:

```python
PEAKS = "../data/peaks/RAD21_ENCFF391AAM.bed.gz"

rule all:
    input:
        "rad21_widths.tsv",

checkpoint split_peaks:
    input:
        PEAKS,
    output:
        directory("rad21_chunks"),
    shell:
        "mkdir -p {output} && zcat {input} | split -l 50 - {output}/chunk_"

rule chunk_width:
    input:
        "rad21_chunks/chunk_{part}",
    output:
        "rad21_widths/{part}.txt",
    shell:
        "awk '{{s += $3 - $2}} END {{print FILENAME, NR, s}}' {input} > {output}"

def chunk_widths(wildcards):
    chunks = checkpoints.split_peaks.get().output[0]
    parts = sorted(glob_wildcards(chunks + "/chunk_{part}").part)
    return expand("rad21_widths/{part}.txt", part=parts)

rule gather_widths:
    input:
        chunk_widths,
    output:
        "rad21_widths.tsv",
    shell:
        "cat {input} > {output}"
```

## What a checkpoint does to the run

The dry run lists 3 jobs: `split_peaks`, `gather_widths`, `all`. It cannot list
`chunk_width`, because the chunks do not exist yet. The real run grows:

```
1 of 3 steps (33%) done
...
2 of 6 steps (33%) done
```

and the result has one line per chunk:

```
rad21_chunks/chunk_aa 50 13783
rad21_chunks/chunk_ab 50 13701
rad21_chunks/chunk_ac 44 11544
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`checkpoints.split_peaks.get()` raises a special exception until the checkpoint
has run. Snakemake catches it, runs the checkpoint, then calls the input
function again and adds the three `chunk_width` jobs. That is the whole trick.

Use a checkpoint only when you really cannot know the outputs up front. If you
could compute the number from the inputs at parse time (the samplesheet, the
config, the size of a file that already exists), do that instead. Checkpoints
make dry runs incomplete, which weakens the tests in module 8.
:::

::: {.notes}
Save this file as `checkpoint-demo/Snakefile` inside the course folder if you
want to run it live; the `../data` path assumes that location. It takes a
couple of seconds.
:::

## What makes a job rerun

By default Snakemake 8 reruns a job when any of these changed since it last ran:

| Trigger | Example |
|---|---|
| `mtime` | an input file is newer than the output |
| `params` | `minMapq` went from 30 to 20 |
| `input` | the set of input files changed |
| `code` | the shell command or script was edited |
| `software-env` | the conda env file changed |

Snakemake stores what it needs to check this in `.snakemake/metadata/`.

## A parameter change, live

Make one filtered BAM, then ask what a stricter MAPQ would rerun:

```bash
snakemake -s workflows/RegPipe.snakefile --cores 4 -- $PWD/output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_filtered.bam
snakemake -n -s workflows/RegPipe.snakefile --cores 1 --config minMapq=20 -- $PWD/output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_filtered.bam
```

{{< generated name="regpipe-params-rerun" command="false" lines="4-33" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Two things in that output. The `filter` job reruns because its params changed
(`before: 30 now: 20`). And `align` reruns too, even though nothing about it
changed: its BAM is `temp()`, so it was deleted after `filter` used it, and
`filter` needs it again. A `temp()` output saves disk and costs you a rerun
whenever something downstream changes.

The `$PWD/` in the target is needed in RegPipe because `OUT` is an absolute
path, so the rules' outputs are absolute. A relative `output/...` on the
command line matches no rule (`MissingRuleException`).
:::

## Turning triggers off

`--rerun-triggers mtime` goes back to the old behavior: only timestamps count.

```bash
snakemake -n ... --rerun-triggers mtime --config minMapq=20 -- $PWD/output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_filtered.bam
```

{{< generated name="regpipe-params-mtime" command="false" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
When is that what you want? We hit one case while building RegPipe: switching
from tools on `PATH` to `--use-conda` changed every rule's software
environment, and Snakemake wanted to rerun everything. If you know the tools
are the same versions either way, `--rerun-triggers mtime` saves that rerun.
Use it when you know the change does not matter, and never as a default.
:::

## Choosing what runs yourself

```bash
bash RegPipe.sh --forcerun call_peaks   # rerun every call_peaks job, and all that depends on them
bash RegPipe.sh --until filter          # run only up to filter: 21 jobs from scratch
bash RegPipe.sh qc_table                # a rule without wildcards can be a target: 34 jobs
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`--forcerun` is what you use after changing something Snakemake cannot see,
such as a MACS3 version installed outside conda. `--until` is handy on a new
cluster: run the cheap first steps and check the logs before you commit hours
of compute. The two job counts are from dry runs on an empty output folder.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .exercise}

## Parameters Snakemake cannot see

The `params` trigger only sees what is in `params:`. ChromSimPipe passes its
scripts one param, the config file's **path**:

```python
    params:
        configfile = CONFIGFILE,
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The scripts read every physics parameter from that file themselves, through
`configs/parameters.py`. Edit a value in the file and the path is the same, so
the params trigger sees no change. The file is not an input either, so `mtime`
does not see it. Nothing reruns, and the old simulations stay in place.

This is a deliberate trade-off. There are dozens of parameters, and passing
them all as params would make every rule long. The repository's
troubleshooting table says to delete the `.done` markers of the steps you want
to redo. The field guide discusses it in
[Parameters](../field-guide/chromsimpipe.qmd#cs-parameters). RegPipe passes
the values themselves (`mapq = config["minMapq"]`), which is why the dry run
above caught the change.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .exercise}

## GPU jobs {#gpu-jobs}

ChromSimPipe's simulations run on a GPU. The rule stays the same everywhere;
only the Longleaf profile asks for one:

{{< snippet repo="chromsimpipe" file="profiles/longleaf/config.yaml" lines="34-40" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`gpu: 1` asks the SLURM plugin for one GPU. The partition list lets SLURM pick
whichever GPU partition has a free node, and the profile also sets the QOS
those partitions use on Longleaf. The point for your own pipelines: a GPU is one more resource, and
like memory and time it goes in the profile, per rule
([GPU](../field-guide/chromsimpipe.qmd#cs-gpu)).
:::

## Key points

- `multiext()` when you know every file name, `directory()` when you do not, a `.done` sentinel only when the files are not Snakemake's to track. Only `multiext()` notices a missing file.
- `rules.X.output` keeps two rules in step when X's outputs change.
- `scattergather:` splits a step into chunks and gathers them; with 4 chunks, RegPipe goes from 61 to 111 jobs with the same results.
- A checkpoint is for outputs you cannot know until a job runs. None of the lab pipelines needs one.
- Snakemake reruns on changed params, code, inputs and envs, not only timestamps. It cannot see values a script reads by itself.
- A `temp()` output is deleted after use, so changing anything downstream reruns the step that made it.
